<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<span id="p1.pic1.p1" class="ltx_para"><img src="2605.13986v2/figures/prior-logo.png" id="p1.pic1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:119/39;" width="119" height="39" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">
<span id="p1.pic1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:173%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-3: Technical Report</span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p1.2" class="ltx_p"><a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Contributors" class="ltx_ref" style="font-size:120%;--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Prior Labs Team</a><span id="p1.pic1.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> (see Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Contributors" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a> for the list of contributors)</span></span>
<span id="p1.pic1.p1.3" class="ltx_p"><span id="p1.pic1.p1.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Tabular data underpins most high-value prediction problems in science and industry, and TabPFN has driven the foundation model revolution for this modality. Designed with feedback from our users, <span id="p1.pic1.p1.3.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> builds on this foundation to scale state-of-the-art performance to datasets with 1M training rows and substantially reduce training and inference time.
Pretrained exclusively on synthetic data from our prior, <span id="p1.pic1.p1.3.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> dramatically pushes the frontier of tabular prediction and brings substantial gains on time series, relational, and tabular-text data.</span></span>
</span>
                
<section id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">A new performance standard.</h5>

<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">On the standard tabular benchmark TabArena, a forward pass of </span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-3</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> outperforms all other models, including tuned and ensembled baselines, by a significant margin, and pareto-dominates the speed/performance frontier. </span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-3</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> also scales to more diverse datasets: it ranks first on datasets with many classes, and beats 8-hour-tuned gradient-boosted-tree baselines on datasets up to 1M training rows and 200 features.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                
<section id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Thinking mode.</h5>

<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-3</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> introduces test-time compute scaling to tabular foundation models. Our API offering </span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-3-Plus</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> (Thinking) exploits this to beat all non-TabPFN models by over 200 Elo on the standard TabArena benchmark, rising to 420 Elo on the largest data subset, and outperforming AutoGluon 1.5 extreme in less than a tenth of its runtime, without using LLMs, real data, internet search or any other model besides TabPFN.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                
<section id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Broader capabilities.</h5>

<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-3 extends the capabilities of our models, enabling SOTA prediction on many-class datasets, relational data (new SOTA foundation model on RelBenchV1) and tabular-text datasets (SOTA on TabSTAR via </span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-3-Plus</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">).
It also directly improves existing integrations of TabPFN:
a specialized </span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-3</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> checkpoint,
TabPFN-TS-3, ranks 2</span><math id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{}^{\text{nd}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msup><mrow></mrow><mtext style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">nd</mtext></msup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{}^{\text{nd}}</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> on the time-series benchmark fev-bench,
and SHAP-value computation through </span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">shapiq</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> is up to </span><math id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="120\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" mathcolor="#000000">120</mn><mo style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;" lspace="0.222em" mathcolor="#000000">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">120\times</annotation></semantics></math><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> faster with KV caching.</span></span>
</span>
</section>
                
<section id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">An enterprise-ready model.</h5>

<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-3</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> achieves this performance while being up to 20x faster than </span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-2.5</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">. In addition, a reduced KV cache and row-chunking scale to 1M rows on a single H100 with fast inference speed.</span></span>
</span>
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">We release TabPFN-3 under the </span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TABPFN-3.0 License v1.0</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">, permissive for research and internal evaluation. </span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TabPFN-3-Plus</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p2.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> (Thinking) is available via API and enterprise licensing including on-prem and VPC environments (AWS SageMaker, Azure AI Foundry).</span></span>
</span>
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#737373;">Date</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> May 12, 2026</span></span>
</span>
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#737373;">License</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">TABPFN-3.0 License v1.0</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> (see Section </span><a href="#S5" title="5 License and Availability" class="ltx_ref" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> for details)</span></span>
</span>
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps" style="font-size:90%;--ltx-fg-color:#737373;">Docs</span><span id="S0.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;"> </span><a href="https://docs.priorlabs.ai" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">https://docs.priorlabs.ai</a></span>

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Tabular data sits at the core of operational decision-making across science and industry, including clinical risk prediction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>, <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>, <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>, credit scoring <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>, <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>, <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>, predictive maintenance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">9</a>, <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">10</a>]</cite>, and scientific measurement <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">11</a>, <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">12</a>]</cite>. While gradient-boosted trees were the reliable default for decades <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">13</a>, <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">14</a>, <a href="#bib.bib155" title="" class="ltx_ref">15</a>]</cite>, tabular foundation models have displaced them as the strongest predictors on standard small-to-medium-sized benchmarks over the last year <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Earlier TabPFN releases established and extended this paradigm. TabPFN v1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> showed that a transformer pretrained on synthetic tasks could approximate Bayesian inference in a single forward pass, though only on a thousand rows of clean numerical data. TabPFN v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> scaled this to 10,000 rows datasets with categorical features, missing values, and outliers, becoming the first tabular foundation model to outperform tuned gradient-boosted trees on standard benchmarks. TabPFN-2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> extended the strong performance to 100,000 rows and 2,000 features and matched four-hour-tuned ensembles in a single forward pass.
Across these releases, an active research ecosystem of extensions grew on top of the core model – domains include time-series forecasting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, causal inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, Bayesian optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, graph learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, interpretability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">26</a>, <a href="#bib.bib156" title="" class="ltx_ref">27</a>]</cite>, reinforcement learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>
– with over 200 published applications (see Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I TabPFN Use Case Overview" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>) and more than three million PyPI downloads.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN-3 is shaped by the feedback from users and the entire ecosystem. To remove common bottlenecks, we scaled beyond a hundred thousand rows to one million rows, cut the memory and latency of inference at scale, added support for many-class classification, and honed our calibrated predictive distributions in a single forward pass.
Furthermore, we carefully designed the TabPFN-3 model
and training process to lift performance on both core tabular prediction as well as the
many downstream extensions built on top of the open-source model, in particular time-series forecasting, multi-table relational data, and interpretability.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The remainder of this report describes the architecture, prior, and inference-time optimizations of TabPFN-3 (Section <a href="#S2" title="2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>); evaluates its performance on public and internal benchmarks across classification, regression, many-class, time-series, and relational data (Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>); surveys the adoption and ecosystem the model is built for (Section <a href="#S4" title="4 Adoption" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>); and details licensing and availability (Section <a href="#S5" title="5 License and Availability" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>). Appendices provide architectural hyperparameters, prior visualizations, additional internal benchmarks, more detailed benchmark results and an extensive list of published TabPFN use cases. For installation and usage, see <a href="https://docs.priorlabs.ai/" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://docs.priorlabs.ai/</a>.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F4.sf1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">(a)</span> </span><span id="S1.F4.sf1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">TabPFN-3 presents a significant improvement against TabPFN-2.5<span id="S1.F4.sf1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. The normalization procedure is described in Section <a href="#A6.SS1" title="F.1 Methodology ‣ Appendix F Additional Details on Internal Benchmarks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.1</span></a>.</span></span></figcaption>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S1.F4.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 4</span>: </span><span id="S1.F4.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Evolution and performance of the TabPFN model family.<span id="S1.F4.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
The row and feature counts in the table denote benchmark-validated regimes
where public and internal evaluations demonstrate state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance;
larger or different row–feature configurations may be feasible, but are outside
the validated SOTA envelope summarized here. Earlier releases are evaluated
within a single row–feature regime, whereas TabPFN-3 is benchmarked along a
cell-budget frontier: up to 1M rows at 200 features, 100k rows at 2,000
features, or 1k rows at 20,000 features. The right panel shows per-dataset
scores across TabArena; points below the diagonal indicate stronger TabPFN-3
performance, with a Wilcoxon test confirming that the improvement is significant
(<math id="S1.F4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="p&lt;0.0001" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>&lt;</mo><mn>0.0001</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">p&lt;0.0001</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>TabPFN-3</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN-3 comes with a new architecture (Section <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Architecture ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>), including an attention-based many-class decoder (Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Many-class Decoder ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>), an improved preprocessing pipeline (Section <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Preprocessing ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>), inference-time optimizations that enable scaling to one million rows on a single GPU (Section <a href="#S2.SS4" title="2.4 Inference Optimization ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4</span></a>), and an improved synthetic SCM prior used for pre-training (Section <a href="#S2.SS5" title="2.5 Synthetic Prior ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.5</span></a>). We also introduce the API and enterprise features <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> which handles text in tables natively and <span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) which applies test-time-compute for dramatically improved performance (Section <a href="#S2.SS6" title="2.6 TabPFN-3-Plus and Thinking mode ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.6</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Architecture</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">An overview of TabPFN-3’s full architecture is shown in <a href="#S2.F5" title="In 2.1 Architecture ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.
TabPFN-3 introduces a substantially redesigned architecture that scales in-context learning to datasets with one million rows.

<br class="ltx_break"></p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN v1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>]</cite> used a transformer architecture to perform in-context learning (ICL) on embeddings of entire rows.
TabPFN-2.x (v2, v2.5, v2.6) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>, <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> used a transformer architecture that alternates row-wise and feature-wise attention layers; this improves performance, but becomes prohibitively expensive as the dataset size grows.
TabPFN-3 returns to TabPFN v1’s ICL for embeddings of entire rows.
It builds on the two-stage row-compression design introduced by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al. [29]</a>, <a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al. [30]</a></cite> in the TabICL architecture, which uses a column-wise feature embedding layer followed by row-wise feature aggregation to obtain the row representation that is used in a TabPFN v1-like ICL layer.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Before entering the two compression stages, we group features, similar to TabPFN-2.x, while adopting TabICLv2’s<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> group assignment, which creates triplets by grouping each feature with two cyclically shifted neighbors. Each triplet is mapped to the hidden dimension of the model by a learned linear projection (cell embedding), and target-aware embeddings are added to the cell embeddings of training rows <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The resulting grouped feature embeddings are processed by the following three stages:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stage 1: Feature distribution embedding (column-wise).</span>
Each feature column is embedded independently using a transformer with an efficient inducing-point attention mechanism.
This avoids the quadratic cost of full cross-row attention while still capturing column-level statistics at arbitrary dataset scales.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stage 2: Feature aggregation (row-wise).</span>
For each data point, a set of learned <span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">cls</span> tokens and the feature embeddings of that row attend to one another via non-causal attention, allowing cross-feature information to be distilled into a fixed number of vectors.
Concatenating the <span id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">cls</span> tokens’ hidden states yields a single, fixed-dimensional embedding per row, decoupling the subsequent in-context learning stage from the number of input features.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Stage 3: In-context learning.</span>
The row embeddings for the training and test sets are jointly passed to a transformer that performs in-context learning: training-row embeddings attend to one another to capture relationships within the training set, while test-row embeddings attend to training-row embeddings to produce predictions.
Because each data point is now a single vector, this stage operates on a sequence proportional only to the number of rows, enabling efficient scaling to large datasets.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p6" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">In Stages 1 and 3, and in the many-class decoder (introduced below), every attention layer applies the query-aware scalable softmax (QASSMax) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, itself inspired from SSMAX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib270" title="" class="ltx_ref">31</a>]</cite>, which rescales attention queries as a function of input length, improving length generalization of in-context learning to large training sets.
Detailed architectural hyperparameters are provided in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Architectural Hyperparameters" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F5" class="ltx_figure">

<div id="S2.SS1.p7" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS1.p7.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN-3 introduces several architectural innovations on top of the three-stage architecture:</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p8" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S2.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attention-based many-class decoder.</span>
For classification, the fixed-width MLP output head of previous TabPFN versions is replaced with an attention-based retrieval decoder that treats class prediction as soft nearest-neighbor retrieval over the in-context training set, inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib276" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arbel et al. [32]</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koshil et al. [33]</a></cite>.
The decoder is non-parametric in the class count, enabling native support for an arbitrary number of classes.
A detailed description is given in Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Many-class Decoder ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Row-chunking.</span> A two-phase inference scheme that decouples peak GPU activation memory from dataset size (rows <math id="S2.I2.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>×</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\times</annotation></semantics></math> columns), while producing outputs equivalent to the unchunked computation: we precompute the distribution embedder’s inducing-vector summary once over the full training set, then stream rows through feature embedding and column aggregation in fixed-size chunks that reuse this cached summary as their attention key/value set. See Section <a href="#S2.SS4.SSS1" title="2.4.1 Row-Chunking ‣ 2.4 Inference Optimization ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4.1</span></a> for more details.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Reduced KV cache via multi-query attention.</span>
In the ICL transformer, test-row queries attend to train-row keys and values using a single KV head (multi-query attention), while train rows retain full multi-head attention.
This allows reducing the per-estimator KV cache to approximately 7 GB for datasets of one million rows, enabling ultra-fast inference on common GPUs. This is described in detail in Section <a href="#S2.SS4.SSS2" title="2.4.2 Fast Inference with a Small KV-cache ‣ 2.4 Inference Optimization ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4.2</span></a>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Orthogonal target embeddings.</span>
Training labels are encoded with learned embeddings initialized via orthogonal decomposition, providing near-maximally separated class representations at the start of training and improving gradient flow in the many-class regime.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">RMSNorm.</span>
All normalization layers use RMSNorm in place of the layer normalization used in <span id="S2.I2.i5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-2.5</span>. RMSNorm omits the mean-centering term, reducing compute while preserving training stability.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I2.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I2.i6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I2.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I2.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Native missing-value handling.</span>
For each cell that is <span id="S2.I2.i6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">NaN</span>, TabPFN-3 computes a binary indicator and concatenates it with the cell value before embedding. The model therefore receives an explicit signal about missing data and can condition its predictions accordingly, rather than relying on upstream imputation.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Many-class Decoder</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For multiclass classification, <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> replaces the fixed-width MLP classification head used in TabPFN-2.6 (and earlier versions) with an <em id="S2.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">attention-based retrieval decoder</em> over the in-context training set,
which treats class prediction as a soft nearest-neighbor retrieval, inspired by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib276" title="" class="ltx_ref">Arbel et al. [32]</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Koshil et al. [33]</a></cite>: the final-layer train embeddings <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{h^{\mathrm{train}}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{train}}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>train</mi></msub></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{h^{\mathrm{train}}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{train}}}</annotation></semantics></math> act as keys, the corresponding one-hot label vectors <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathbf{y}_{n}\in\{0,1\}^{C}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>𝐲</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow><mi>C</mi></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathbf{y}_{n}\in\{0,1\}^{C}</annotation></semantics></math> as values, and test embeddings <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="h^{\mathrm{test}}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi><mi>test</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">h^{\mathrm{test}}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math> as queries. After the usual learned linear projections <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{Q},W_{K}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>K</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{Q},W_{K}</annotation></semantics></math> and a multi-head split, the decoder computes</p>
<table id="S2.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">

k^{(h)}_{n}}{\sqrt{D_{h}}}\right),</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">that is: a (head-averaged) attention-weighted average of the in-context one-hot labels, which is then converted to logits via <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log\!\big(\mathrm{clip}(p_{m})\big)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mpadded style="width:1.146em;" width="1.146em"><mi>log</mi></mpadded><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">(</mo><mrow><mi>clip</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="1.200em" minsize="1.200em">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log\!\big(\mathrm{clip}(p_{m})\big)</annotation></semantics></math>. This formulation has two consequences. First, classes are no longer tied to fixed output positions of a parametric head
so the decoder is naturally permutation-equivariant in the class indices.
Second, decoding is non-parametric in <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>: the decoder’s parameters depend only on the embedding dimension and the number of attention heads, not on some <math id="S2.SS2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math>, decoupling the head’s capacity from the supported label cardinality.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Class-count limit from pre-training.</span>
Although the decoder is non-parametric in <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>C</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C</annotation></semantics></math>, the trained <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> still fixes a hard ceiling <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\max}=160" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>160</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\max}=160</annotation></semantics></math> at pre-training time via three checkpoint-bound tensors: the trainable orthogonal label embeddings <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="E_{\mathrm{col}},E_{\mathrm{icl}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{\max}\times D}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>col</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>icl</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><msup><mi>ℝ</mi><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">E_{\mathrm{col}},E_{\mathrm{icl}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C_{\max}\times D}</annotation></semantics></math> used by the column encoder and the ICL transformer, and the one-hot value tensor consumed by the decoder. Enlarging <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="C_{\max}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C_{\max}</annotation></semantics></math> at pre-training therefore costs only <math id="S2.SS2.p2.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{O}(C_{\max}\,D)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">𝒪</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>max</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{O}(C_{\max}\,D)</annotation></semantics></math> extra parameters and no extra decode-time memory.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.3 </span>Preprocessing</h3>

<div id="S2.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As in previous versions, TabPFN-3 aggregates predictions across multiple estimators, each operating on a distinct combination of dataset permutations and feature transformations, forming an effective ensemble that enhances robustness and generalization. Individual estimators apply complementary feature transformations—combining robust scaling and soft clipping (following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>) with quantile transformations and standard scaling—to balance stability and sensitivity across varying feature distributions. As in TabPFN-2.5, a subset of estimators augments the feature matrix with singular value decomposition (SVD) components, capturing high-energy directions of global variance.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN-3 introduces two further improvements to this pipeline. First, features are subsampled in a round-robin fashion, ensuring that each feature appears in at least one estimator and is never systematically excluded from the ensemble. For datasets exceeding 100,000 rows, random feature subsampling is replaced by an informed selection based on Gini importance derived from a lightweight tree model fitted on a subsample, focusing each estimator on the most discriminative features rather than an arbitrary subset. Second, feature transformations such as quantile normalization are now executed on GPU, substantially reducing preprocessing latency and making the pipeline practical at the larger dataset scales supported by TabPFN-3. As in TabPFN-2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, post-processing capabilities are available, including decision threshold tuning for metric-specific optimization (e.g., F1-score) and temperature scaling for probability calibration.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.4 </span>Inference Optimization</h3>

<div id="S2.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> introduces several inference-time optimizations that together reduce its compute and memory footprint enough to scale to one-million-rows on a single GPU with sub-second inference latency.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.4.1 </span>Row-Chunking</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span>’s pre-ICL stages—cell embedding, feature distribution embedding, and feature aggregation—materialize an <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="(n_{\mathrm{train}}+n_{\mathrm{test}}){\times}n_{\mathrm{features}}{\times}d" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>test</mi></msub></mrow><mo rspace="0.055em" stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo rspace="0.222em">×</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(n_{\mathrm{train}}+n_{\mathrm{test}}){\times}n_{\mathrm{features}}{\times}d</annotation></semantics></math> activation, so peak memory can saturate the GPU well before any operation becomes compute-bound. One solution is to offload activations to CPU memory or disk, as in TabICLv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>. This however requires a large amount of CPU memory (250GB for a <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1\text{M}\times 500" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mtext>M</mtext></mrow><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">×</mo><mn>500</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1\text{M}\times 500</annotation></semantics></math> table in <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al. [30]</a></cite>), or otherwise incurs substantial I/O overhead (<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qu et al. [30]</a></cite> report a 4x slowdown).
We instead stream the row dimension in fixed-size slices and keep all activations on the GPU.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F6" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/chunked_vs_nonchunked_h100.svg" id="S2.F6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/247;" width="476" height="247"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F6.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 6</span>: </span><span id="S2.F6.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Chunking flattens the peak-memory without impacting the time-per-call.<span id="S2.F6.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Model forward pass without preprocessing, measured on a H100, for <math id="S2.F6.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{features}}\in\{10,100,500\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">{</mo><mn>10,100,500</mn><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{features}}\in\{10,100,500\}</annotation></semantics></math>. Top row: peak GPU memory (GiB) versus number of training rows; bottom row: time per call (ms). Three series per panel: <span id="S2.F6.9.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> without chunking (blue), <span id="S2.F6.9.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> with chunking (pink), and the <span id="S2.F6.9.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-2.5</span> baseline (black). Both axes are log-scaled.
Note that <em id="S2.F6.9.1.4" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">TabPFN-3 is much faster than TabPFN-2.5, especially at large feature counts.</em></span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A naive row-wise stream is not directly applicable: the distribution embedder summarizes the training set into a fixed-size<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              We use 128 inducing points, much smaller than the dataset sizes of interest, which often exceed 100,000 rows.</span></span></span> set of inducing points via cross-attention over all training rows, and splitting that call across chunks would change its semantics. <span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> resolves this with a two-phase scheme exactly equivalent to the unchunked computation: (i) the inducing states are computed once over the full training set, chunked along the (independent) column dimension to bound its own memory cost; (ii) rows are then streamed through feature distribution embedding and the feature aggregator in fixed-size chunks, each reusing the precomputed inducing states as its attention key/value set, and the per-chunk row embeddings are concatenated along the row axis. The scheme adds a small overhead from recomputing cell embeddings in phase (ii) but avoids the disk-bandwidth bottleneck. We enable chunking when <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{train}}+n_{\mathrm{test}}&gt;2048" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>test</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mn>2048</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{train}}+n_{\mathrm{test}}&gt;2048</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S2.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ 2.4.1 Row-Chunking ‣ 2.4 Inference Optimization ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> highlights the different memory–compute trade-offs of <span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> and <span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-2.5</span>. Without chunking, the peak memory of <span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> grows steeply with <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{features}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{features}}</annotation></semantics></math>. This is because the model carries a pre-ICL activation <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{features}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{features}}</annotation></semantics></math>-wide through cell embedding, feature distribution embedding, and feature aggregation before collapsing the feature axis into a single row representation for the ICL transformer. By contrast, <span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-2.5</span> alternates row- and column-attention layers over a representation grouped into <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{features}}/3" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{features}}/3</annotation></semantics></math> tokens, and therefore never materialises a tensor wider than this. This explains why <span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span>’s unchunked peak memory exceeds <span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-2.5</span>’s. Applying row-chunking to <span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> flattens peak memory with respect to <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{features}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{features}}</annotation></semantics></math> and yields an approximately <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m6" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="{\sim}5{\times}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>∼</mo><mn>5</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}5{\times}</annotation></semantics></math> reduction at the largest shapes, enabling 1M-row inference, while incurring only a small wall-clock overhead of a few percent near <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{train}}\approx 10^{4}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><mo>≈</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{train}}\approx 10^{4}</annotation></semantics></math> that becomes amortised at larger scales once the <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{train}}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{train}}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> ICL row-attention dominates. At the same time, the feature-collapsed row representation gives <span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> a substantial runtime advantage at large <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{train}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{train}}</annotation></semantics></math> or <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{features}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{features}}</annotation></semantics></math> since its ICL row-attention scales as <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m11" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{train}}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{train}}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math> independently of <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m12" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{features}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{features}}</annotation></semantics></math>, whereas <span id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.1.9" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-2.5</span>’s row attention retains linear dependence on <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m13" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{features}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{features}}</annotation></semantics></math> and scales with <math id="S2.SS4.SSS1.p3.m14" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{features}}\cdot n_{\mathrm{train}}^{2}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{features}}\cdot n_{\mathrm{train}}^{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>

<section id="S2.SS4.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.4.2 </span>Fast Inference with a Small KV-cache</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Being an in-context-learning model, <span id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> combines training (fit) and inference (predict) in one forward pass. While this allows for very fast training, it can make online or batched predictions too slow for production usecases. Caching the keys and values (KVs) from the train set removes this issue. While KV-caching has been available in our previous models, the memory cost of the cache was prohibitive for larger datasets. <span id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> solves this in two ways:</p>
<ul id="S2.I3" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I3.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I3.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Compared to <span id="S2.I3.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-2.5</span>, which needs to store an embedding for each cell of the table, <span id="S2.I3.i1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> only needs to store three components: the per-block inducing states produced by the feature distribution embedder, the train-side keys and values of the ICL self-attention at every transformer block in the ICL stage; as well as the train embeddings of the final ICL layer, which are consumed by the many-class decoder. The inducing states are small and the two other components only scale with the number of rows rather than rows × features.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I3.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I3.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I3.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use multi-query with only a single head for cross attention between test and train samples, reducing KV-cache size by a factor of eight.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This achieves a KV-cache size of 7GiB per estimator for 1M rows datasets, making <span id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.2.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span>’s default 8 estimators usable on common GPUs even for the largest datasets we support. As can be seen in Figure <a href="#S2.F7.sf1" title="Figure 7(a) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 2.4.1 Row-Chunking ‣ 2.4 Inference Optimization ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7(a)</span></a>, peak memory of (chunked) cache-predict is basically flat across feature sizes.
On an H100, cached-predict is one to three orders of magnitude faster than either the <span id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.2.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-2.5</span> baseline or <span id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.2.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span>’s own cold “fit+predict” path (Figure <a href="#S2.F7.sf2" title="Figure 7(b) ‣ Figure 7 ‣ 2.4.1 Row-Chunking ‣ 2.4 Inference Optimization ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7(b)</span></a>), achieving between 0.1 and 3 ms/test point for batches of 100 test points. The fit-with-cache call costs essentially the same as the cold fit+predict at every measured shape, including <math id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{train}}=10^{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{train}}=10^{6}</annotation></semantics></math> where both complete in <math id="S2.SS4.SSS2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="{\sim}107" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>∼</mo><mn>107</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">{\sim}107</annotation></semantics></math> s (Figure <a href="#S2.F8" title="Figure 8 ‣ 2.4.2 Fast Inference with a Small KV-cache ‣ 2.4 Inference Optimization ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F8" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/H100_kv_cache_scaling.svg" id="S2.F8.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:405/135;" width="405" height="135"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F8.13" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 8</span>: </span><span id="S2.F8.14" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">TabPFN-3</span><span id="S2.F8.15" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">’s KV-cached predict allows for one to three orders of magnitude speedup<span id="S2.F8.15.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. We report results for a single estimator without preprocessing on an H100, for <math id="S2.F8.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{features}}\in\{10,100\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>features</mi></msub><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">{</mo><mn>10,100</mn><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{features}}\in\{10,100\}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.F8.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{test}}=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>test</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{test}}=100</annotation></semantics></math>. Four series per panel: <span id="S2.F8.15.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-2.5</span> <span id="S2.F8.15.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">fit+predict</span> (black, baseline), <span id="S2.F8.15.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> cold <span id="S2.F8.15.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">fit+predict</span> (blue, no cache reuse), <span id="S2.F8.15.1.5" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> <span id="S2.F8.15.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">fit (build cache)</span> that builds the cache (magenta – overlaps the cold curve since the train-side work is identical, the cache is just retained), and <span id="S2.F8.15.1.7" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> cached <span id="S2.F8.15.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">predict</span> (yellow). The KV-Cache is built under the deployed multi-query test-side configuration (<math id="S2.F8.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{kv,test}}=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>kv</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>test</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{kv,test}}=1</annotation></semantics></math>).</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.4.3 </span>Model Distillation</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In production environments constrained by latency or memory budgets, hardware availability, or regulatory requirements that mandate familiar model classes, <span id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> also supports distillation into dataset-specific MLPs or tree ensembles via the engine introduced with <span id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-2.5</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>. The distilled artifact runs on CPU at the sub-millisecond latency of a standard MLP or tree ensemble while retaining most of <span id="S2.SS4.SSS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span>’s predictive performance on the dataset it was distilled for.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.4.4 </span>Compilation and FlashAttention-3</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> ships with two opt-in performance features that target different bottlenecks: <span id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">torch.compile</span>, which fuses dispatch on the non-attention hot paths, and FlashAttention-3 (FA3) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib142" title="" class="ltx_ref">35</a>]</cite>, a Hopper-specific kernel for the in-context-learning attention. On MI-250x, <span id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">torch.compile</span> reaches up to <math id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.58{\times}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.58</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.58{\times}</annotation></semantics></math> speedup on the non-chunked forward pass; on H100, FA3 reaches <math id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p1.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="1.5\text{--}1.7{\times}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>1.5</mn><mtext>–</mtext><mn>1.7</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.5\text{--}1.7{\times}</annotation></semantics></math> at <math id="S2.SS4.SSS4.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="n_{\mathrm{train}}=10^{6}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>train</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mn>10</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">n_{\mathrm{train}}=10^{6}</annotation></semantics></math> over the SDPA fallback. Both compose cleanly with row chunking and are auto-detected at runtime; see Appendix <a href="#A7.SS1" title="G.1 Compilation and FlashAttention-3 ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Inference Time Details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G.1</span></a> for the full measurements and per-shape breakdowns.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS4.SSS5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">2.4.5 </span>Improved interpretability for TabPFN</h4>

<div id="S2.SS4.SSS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN-3’s reduced KV-cache (Section <a href="#S2.SS4.SSS2" title="2.4.2 Fast Inference with a Small KV-cache ‣ 2.4 Inference Optimization ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4.2</span></a>) and fast inference make interpretability extensions significantly more practical.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS4.SSS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS4.SSS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Through the <span id="S2.SS4.SSS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tabpfn-extensions</span> package, TabPFN is directly integrated with the popular <span id="S2.SS4.SSS5.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">shapiq</span> library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib138" title="" class="ltx_ref">36</a>]</cite>, enabling efficient approximation of any-order Shapley interactions. <a href="#A7.F38" title="Figure 38 ‣ G.2 Interpretability: SHAP-Value Computation ‣ Appendix G Supplementary Inference Time Details" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 38</span></a> in the Appendix shows both the absolute runtime and the relative speed-ups achieved by KV caching. For large datasets, KV caching provides more than <math id="S2.SS4.SSS5.p2.m1" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="120\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>120</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">120\times</annotation></semantics></math> efficiency gains, reducing the runtime per test row to 1.08 seconds even for a training table with 200k rows and 500 features.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.5 </span>Synthetic Prior</h3>

<div id="S2.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following previous TabPFN model variants <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>, <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">16</a>, <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>, TabPFN-3 is trained on synthetically generated data based on our Structural Causal Model (SCM) prior. A schematic flow chart demonstrating how our SCM prior works is shown in Figure <a href="#S2.F9" title="Figure 9 ‣ 2.5 Synthetic Prior ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our philosophy in designing our prior is to maximize breadth of possible datasets while capturing the structure models will encounter in real-world data. The result is an updated, more sophisticated prior that allows us to scale up training and continue extracting signal from the wide range of synthetic datasets it generates: our final TabPFN-3 model was trained on more than 8 trillion tokens.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS5.2" class="ltx_logical-block">
