</div>
        
<figure id="S2.F9" class="ltx_figure ltx_align_center">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S2.F9.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 9</span>: </span><span id="S2.F9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Schematic visualization of our SCM prior.<span id="S2.F9.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> (i) We first sample high-level hyperparameters for the dataset, including number of features and number of rows. (ii) Based on the hyperparameters, we utilize our graph sampling algorithms to generate a directed acyclic graph (DAG) underlying our SCM; in parallel, an i.i.d. noise sample <math id="S2.F9.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\varepsilon_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>ε</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\varepsilon_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is drawn per node (each colour shade in the lower-left mini-panel corresponds to a different node). (iii) We compute a topological ordering of the DAG. Based on this, we create a computational graph: First we fill root nodes (i.e. exogenous variables) and subsequently traverse the computational graph in topological order, combining parent nodes using our combiner mechanisms and activations to propagate values to the child nodes. (iv) We choose suitable features and target variables from our fully computed SCM. (v) We apply post-processing to the dataset.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
      
</div>
<div id="S2.SS5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ol id="S2.I4" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S2.I4.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I4.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I4.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Graph generation.</span> We expand the distribution of graphs
underlying the SCM by introducing new sampling algorithms, enabling
richer structural diversity. Sample graphs are shown in
Figure <a href="#A4.F23" title="Figure 23 ‣ Appendix D Prior visualizations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">23</span></a>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I4.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I4.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I4.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Combiner mechanisms.</span> We introduce a host of new combiner mechanisms that combine values of parent nodes to propagate values to child nodes, some examples of which are visualized for a simple two-dimensional case in Figure <a href="#A4.F24" title="Figure 24 ‣ Appendix D Prior visualizations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">24</span></a>. Increasing the variety of functional forms by which child nodes depend on the respective parent nodes allows for richer node relationships in the SCM.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I4.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I4.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I4.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Categorical variables.</span> Compared to TabPFN-2.5, we reworked the treatment of categorical variables in our SCM, moving from a comparatively simple categorical data model to more expressive variants.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I4.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I4.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I4.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">High-frequency oscillators.</span> TabPFN-2.5 struggled with
high-frequency oscillations despite performing well on sinusoidal data
generally. Improved sinusoidal activations give TabPFN-3 strong
performance across the full frequency spectrum.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I4.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">5.</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I4.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I4.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Spatial prior.</span> Many tabular datasets have underlying spatial structure (e.g. datasets containing longitude and latitude as covariates, grids of sensors, etc.). We add spatial activations that allow our prior to encode spatial relationships between variables.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I4.i6" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">6.</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I4.i6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I4.i6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Many-class prior.</span> The flexible many-class decoder in TabPFN-3 enables native classification support for an arbitrary number of classes. We match this architectural design in the prior, ensuring high quality datasets that enable state-of-the-art downstream performance from binary datasets to datasets with hundreds of classes.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I4.i7" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">7.</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I4.i7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I4.i7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Temporal prior.</span> Many tabular datasets have temporal structure: rows are collected over intervals of time, train and test splits are often ordered by time rather than drawn i.i.d., and temporal dependencies between variables are common. We extend the SCM into a discrete-time Dynamic Structural Causal Model <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib143" title="" class="ltx_ref">37</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I4.i8" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">8.</span> 
<div id="S2.I4.i8.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.I4.i8.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.I4.i8.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Out-of-distribution prior.</span> We add out-of-distribution prediction tasks, allowing models trained on our prior data to remain performant under distribution shifts, as well as moving from pure interpolation to extrapolation. A simple example highlighting how our o.o.d. prior allows <span id="S2.I4.i8.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> to perform extrapolation is shown in Figure <a href="#A4.F26" title="Figure 26 ‣ Appendix D Prior visualizations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">26</span></a> - a capability that is notably absent from most tree-based algorithms as well as most other tabular foundation models.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.6 </span>TabPFN-3-Plus and Thinking mode</h3>

<div id="S2.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">On top of <span id="S2.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span>, which we release open-source, our API and enterprise deployments provide access to <span id="S2.SS6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> and its thinking mode "TabPFN-3-Plus (Thinking)" (named TabPFN-3-Thinking in our plots)
These variants are fully compatible with the open-source <span id="S2.SS6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> interface and can be used as a drop-in replacement, while offering additional capabilities:</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Native text-feature support.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> accepts string-valued columns directly, without requiring upstream featurization. Free-text fields – such as product names, insurance claim descriptions, or customer reviews – are encoded jointly with numeric and categorical features inside the model, so cross-feature interactions between text and structured columns are learned end-to-end rather than imposed by a fixed encoder.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Thinking mode.</h5>

<div id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) applies additional inference-time computation on top of <span id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> to push prediction quality further. Thinking mode composes with native text-feature support, so a single call can handle mixed numerical, categorical, and text columns under the same inference-time-compute regime. We emphasize that our Thinking mode achieves this strong performance while only relying on TabPFN, without using LLMs, real data, internet search, or any other model.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS6.SSS0.Px2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span>, including Thinking mode, is available through our API and through enterprise deployments including on-prem and VPC deployment on AWS SageMaker and Azure AI Foundry; see Section <a href="#S5" title="5 License and Availability" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> for licensing and access. Benchmark results are reported in Sections <a href="#S3.SS1.SSS1" title="3.1.1 TabArena ‣ 3.1 Public Tabular Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.1</span></a> (TabArena), <a href="#S3.SS1.SSS3" title="3.1.3 TabSTAR ‣ 3.1 Public Tabular Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1.3</span></a> (TabSTAR), and <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS1" title="3.2.1 Large Data ‣ 3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.1</span></a> (Large data).</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Experimental Results</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we report experimental results across a variety of benchmarks. In Section <a href="#S3.SS1" title="3.1 Public Tabular Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.1</span></a>, we focus on public tabular benchmarks: TabArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, TALENT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib140" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>, and the text-tabular TabSTAR collection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>. Section <a href="#S3.SS2" title="3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2</span></a> describes internal benchmarks spanning various subtypes of tabular learning, including large-scale datasets and features, many-class classification, and quantile regression. The subsequent sections extend beyond classic tabular learning: Section <a href="#S3.SS3" title="3.3 Time-Series Forecasting ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.3</span></a> addresses time-series data, Section <a href="#S3.SS4" title="3.4 Relational Data ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.4</span></a> covers relational learning, and Section <a href="#S3.SS6" title="3.6 Embeddings ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.6</span></a> focuses on embeddings.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Public Tabular Benchmarks</h3>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.1 </span>TabArena</h4>

<figure id="S3.F10" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/x1.svg" id="S3.F10.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/161;" width="476" height="161"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F10.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 10</span>: </span><span id="S3.F10.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">TabPFN-3 performance on the standard TabArena benchmark<span id="S3.F10.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, including all 51 datasets (up to 100K rows). TabPFN-3 outperforms any other model in a forward pass, while <span id="S3.F10.6.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) strongly outperforms all existing methods, including AutoGluon 1.5 extreme <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, a complex ensemble of models including TabPFN v2 tuned for 4 hours, in less than a tenth of the runtime.
</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TabArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> (NeurIPS 2025 Datasets &amp; Benchmarks) is a recent and heavily curated tabular benchmark, based on the largest number of candidate datasets considered, and created and maintained by open-source contributors from a wide range of institutions.
In particular, it compares a large and regularly updated list of recent models, including tree-based models like CatBoost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>, LightGBM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite> or XGBoost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>, as well as newer deep-learning models like RealMLP <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">34</a>]</cite>, TabM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">43</a>]</cite>, ModernNCA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">44</a>]</cite> or xRFM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">45</a>]</cite>, the AutoML system AutoGluon <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>]</cite>, and other Tabular Foundation Models like TabICL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">29</a>, <a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, TabDPT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib136" title="" class="ltx_ref">46</a>]</cite>, TabSTAR <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>, LimiX <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">47</a>]</cite>, Mitra <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">48</a>]</cite> or TabPFN v2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>.
The benchmark contains a set of 51 datasets selected from 1053 to be representative of real-world tabular data. See <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Erickson et al. [1]</a></cite> for the list of datasets and Section <a href="#A5.SS2.SSS1" title="E.2.1 Evaluation Metrics ‣ E.2 Detailed TabArena Results ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.2.1</span></a> for definitions of TabArena’s Elo and Improvability metrics.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F12" class="ltx_figure">

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Pushing the performance frontier on TabArena.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F10" title="Figure 10 ‣ 3.1.1 TabArena ‣ 3.1 Public Tabular Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a> shows the performance of <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) on TabArena.
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> outperforms in one forward pass all other models, including tuned and ensembled baselines, by a significant margin, gaining 72 Elo points over our previous Real-TabPFN-2.5 tuned and ensembled.
<span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking), leveraging test-time computation, significantly outperforms open-source <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> on TabArena, beating any non-TabPFN model (including tuned and ensembled baselines) by over 200 Elo points,
and outperforming AutoGluon 1.5 extreme, a complex ensemble of models including TabPFN v2, tuned for 4 hours, by over 100 Elo points while being 10x faster.
Looking at the win rate matrix in Figure <a href="#S3.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ 3.1.1 TabArena ‣ 3.1 Public Tabular Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, we can see that <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> with Thinking mode (respectively <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span>) has over 93% (respectively 80%) win rate against tuned and ensembled CatBoost, LightGBM and XGBoost, and a 69% (respectively 56%) win rate against AutoGluon 1.5 extreme tuned for 4 hours.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Dominating the time / performance Pareto-frontier.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The strong results of our models are achieved while being much faster to train than the baselines.
On Figure <a href="#S3.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ 3.1.1 TabArena ‣ 3.1 Public Tabular Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a>, we can see that our model family, (<span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> with 1, 2, and 4 estimators and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> with Thinking mode) strictly dominates the combined training + inference time/performance pareto-frontier on TabArena by a large margin.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scaling to larger datasets.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> was built to scale to large datasets, and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) benefits from this scalability. While TabArena only contains datasets up to 100k rows, we can still observe very strong performance on the 15 largest datasets in TabArena with between 10k and 100k rows, as shown in Figure <a href="#S0.F1" title="Figure 1" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>.
In particular, on this subset <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> outperforms any other model by 100 Elo, and <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) dramatically outperforms any other non-TabPFN model (including tuned and ensembled baselines) by over 420 Elo points, and beats AutoGluon 1.5 extreme (4h) by 220 Elo points.
Looking at the win rate matrix in Figure <a href="#S0.F3" title="Figure 3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS1.Px3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) has over 99% win rate against tuned and ensembled LightGBM and XGBoost, 98% win rate against CatBoost tuned and ensembled, and 82% win rate against AutoGluon 1.5 extreme tuned for 4 hours. In Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS1" title="3.2.1 Large Data ‣ 3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.1</span></a>, we study the performance of our model beyond 100K rows, going up to 1M training rows.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.2 </span>TALENT</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The TALENT benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib140" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> provides a complementary view on the performance of <span id="S3.SS1.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span>. Instead of a smaller curated list of datasets, this benchmark uses a large number of diverse datasets (300) from a wide range of domains. The strong results of TabPFN-3 on this benchmark confirm the robustness of its performance.
Indeed, TabPFN-3 ranks first on the TALENT benchmark in aggregate, as shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F13" title="Figure 13 ‣ 3.1.2 TALENT ‣ 3.1 Public Tabular Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>, as well as for
each task type (regression, binary and multiclass classification) in Figure <a href="#A5.F28" title="Figure 28 ‣ E.3.2 Per-task-type breakdown ‣ E.3 Details on TALENT benchmark results ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">28</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F13" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/average_rank_horizontal_paper.svg" id="S3.F13.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:429/183;" width="429" height="183"></object>

</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.1.3 </span>TabSTAR</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The TabSTAR study <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite> assembled 50 text-tabular datasets, gathered from previous work <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>, <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">50</a>, <a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>. These datasets represent real world tasks, where at least one feature is text-based and cannot be faithfully represented without text processing methods. While the open-source version of <span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> only supports numerical and categorical variables, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> also offers native support for text features. We compare TabPFN API models with both text-aware models and numerical-only baselines.
Figure <a href="#S3.F14" title="Figure 14 ‣ 3.1.3 TabSTAR ‣ 3.1 Public Tabular Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> shows that <span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> dominates the leaderboard by a significant margin, and combining our thinking mode with native text support pushes performance further. Furthermore, among models that omit text features due to lack of native support, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> remains the top performer. Appendix <a href="#A5.SS4" title="E.4 Details on TabSTAR Text-Tabular Benchmark results ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.4</span></a> provides further details on the benchmark, as well as a performance breakdown by task type.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F14" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/tabstar_leaderboard.svg" id="S3.F14.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/200;" width="381" height="200"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F14.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 14</span>: </span><span id="S3.F14.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Performance over the TabSTAR Text-Tabular Collection<span id="S3.F14.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">. <span id="S3.F14.6.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) and TabPFN-3-Plus significantly outperform text-aware models such as CatBoost, TabSTAR and SAP-RPT-OSS. In turn, these models dominate over numerical-only baselines, for which TabPFN-3 gets the best results.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Internal Benchmarks</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To complement the public TabArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> and
TALENT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib140" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> benchmarks, we evaluate TabPFN-3 on a
set of internal benchmarks designed to stress capabilities that are only
partially covered by existing public evaluations. These benchmarks test
whether TabPFN-3 pushes the frontier of tabular foundation models beyond the
small- and medium-data regimes emphasized in prior work. In particular, we
evaluate scaling to more than one million samples, high-dimensional feature
spaces, many-class classification, and quantile regression.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our primary comparisons are against the leading gradient boosted tree frameworks XGBoost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">42</a>]</cite>, CatBoost <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">40</a>]</cite>, and LightGBM <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">41</a>]</cite>, as well as TabICLv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, a recent foundation model for tabular data with strong results on public benchmarks.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1 </span>Large Data</h4>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation Protocol.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The primary baselines for our large-data evaluation are tree-based methods, which recent large-scale tabular benchmarks have shown to be highly competitive beyond 100,000 samples <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib140" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite>. Our large-data benchmarking effort focuses on datasets with 100,000 to 1 million training rows and up to 200 features.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This benchmark targets the large-row regime for which <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> was designed. As described in Section <a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Architecture ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a>, <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> first compresses feature information into fixed-dimensional row representations and subsequently performs in-context learning over these rows.
This architectural decomposition enables inference on datasets with up to one million rows on a single GPU.
At the same time, it induces a scaling trade-off: when both the number of rows and the number of features are very large, the early compression of feature information can become a bottleneck.
We treat the high-dimensional, low-sample regime as a separate evaluation setting, studied in Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS3" title="3.2.3 Many Features ‣ 3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.3</span></a>, rather than conflating it with the large-row setting considered here.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our benchmark datasets span diverse real-world domains including healthcare,
finance, logistics, and environmental science. For regression, the datasets in our benchmark exhibit temporal structure, where models are trained on past data and must generalize to future data. We found this setting to be the most common and representative of real-world deployment conditions.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Results.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> achieves state-of-the-art performance on our large-data benchmark, outperforming default and 8-hour-tuned
gradient-boosted tree baselines in a single forward pass, as shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F15" title="Figure 15 ‣ Results. ‣ 3.2.1 Large Data ‣ 3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a>. Further, we show a preview version of <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) on large data, which improves <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> performance further for classification datasets (as <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> with Thinking mode does not yet support temporal datasets as of the time of writing, we could not evaluate it on our regression benchmark). To better understand how <span id="S3.SS2.SSS1.Px2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> performance scales with training size, we report performance on subsampled versions of our datasets (keeping test set constant, and only considering datasets with 1M training samples) in Figure  <a href="#S3.F16" title="Figure 16 ‣ Results. ‣ 3.2.1 Large Data ‣ 3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>. Across the 100k–1M range, TabPFN-3 scales smoothly and retains the top normalized score at every training-set size.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F15" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.2 </span>Many-Class Classification</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> introduces a many-class decoder (Section <a href="#S2.SS2" title="2.2 Many-class Decoder ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.2</span></a>) that we trained to support up to 160 classes, a regime where most tabular foundation models fail entirely. Creating a benchmark from real-world datasets with naturally many classes is challenging; we therefore evaluate on a synthetic benchmark derived by bucketing regression targets from real regression benchmark datasets. We also confirm the strong performance of <span id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> on the 4 datasets from the TALENT benchmark that have more than 50 classes in Section <a href="#A5.SS3.SSS3" title="E.3.3 Many-class TALENT subset ‣ E.3 Details on TALENT benchmark results ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.3.3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Synthetic many-class benchmark.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We construct
a synthetic benchmark by converting the TabArena regression datasets into many-class
classification problems via jittered quantile binning; full construction details
are given in Appendix <a href="#A6.SS3" title="F.3 Synthetic Many-Class Benchmark Construction ‣ Appendix F Additional Details on Internal Benchmarks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F.3</span></a>.
Figure <a href="#S3.F17" title="Figure 17 ‣ Synthetic many-class benchmark. ‣ 3.2.2 Many-Class Classification ‣ 3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> shows the ROC-AUC (OvR) and accuracy.
TabPFN-3 achieves the highest normalized ROC-AUC of <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.00" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.00</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.00</annotation></semantics></math>, ranking first overall and outperforming all baselines by a large margin.
On ROC-AUC (OvR), the next best model is TabICLv2 at <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.89" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.89</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.89</annotation></semantics></math> using its many-class wrapper to go beyond its 10 classes limit. TabPFN-2.5 achieves <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0.83" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>0.83</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0.83</annotation></semantics></math>, using its own many-class error-correcting-code-based wrapper<span id="footnote2" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup>

Conventional tree-based methods and KNN all perform notably worse, even after <math id="S3.SS2.SSS2.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math> hour of tuning.</p>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.3 </span>Many Features</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The high-dimensional, low-sample regime poses a qualitatively different challenge from the large-row setting studied in Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS1" title="3.2.1 Large Data ‣ 3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.1</span></a>. Whereas large-row benchmarks primarily test scalability to many training examples, the many-features setting tests robust generalization and feature-subset selection when the number of candidate features far exceeds the number of samples.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate this setting on a dedicated <em id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">many-features</em> slice of six real-world classification datasets with 100–320 samples, 1,100–22,200 features, and 2–4 classes, mostly from biomedical or gene-expression-style domains. Such large feature-to-sample ratios are challenging for tree-based methods because they increase the risk of selecting spurious feature interactions.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F19" title="Figure 19 ‣ 3.2.3 Many Features ‣ 3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a> shows that <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> performs strongly on this challenging slice, reaching the best normalized ROC-AUC with 32 estimators.
Earlier TabPFN variants, in particular Real-TabPFN-2.5 and TabPFN v2, also perform competitively, suggesting that TabPFN-style pretraining provides a robust inductive bias for high-dimensional, low-sample problems.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">As described in Section <a href="#S2.SS3" title="2.3 Preprocessing ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.3</span></a>, each <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> estimator is restricted to at most 200 input features per default. Thus, for datasets with tens of thousands of raw features, individual estimators operate on feature subsets rather than compressing the full feature set.
At the same estimator budget, Real-TabPFN-2.5 can slightly outperform <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span>; we hypothesize that this reflects two factors: Real-TabPFN-2.5 uses up to 500 features per estimator, providing broader feature-space coverage on some datasets, and its alternating row-wise and feature-wise attention may better exploit the selected feature subset.
For <span id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span>, increasing the number of estimators improves coverage of the raw feature space and raises the probability that informative feature subsets are included.
In our OSS version, this estimator budget is scaled automatically for high-dimensional inputs, making the ensemble substantially more effective in this regime.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p5" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Overall, the many-features slice suggests that TabPFN estimators can be ensembled effectively in a high-noise feature-selection regime, where conventional tree-based methods are prone to overfitting to noisy or spurious feature interactions.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F19" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F19.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_minipage ltx_align_center ltx_align_top" style="width:165.6pt;"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/many_feats_1k_25k_multiclass_v2__roc_auc_normalized.svg" id="S3.F19.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/162;" width="229" height="162"></object>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS4" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.4 </span>Quantile Regression</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Beyond point predictions, TabPFN-3 provides full predictive distributions via a
bar-distribution regression head (Section <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Architectural Hyperparameters" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>), from
which arbitrary quantiles are decoded at inference by inverting the predicted CDF —
all from a single forward pass, with no retraining per quantile level. Since TabArena does not natively support quantile regression evaluation, we construct
a dedicated benchmark by downloading the TabArena regression datasets and evaluating
all models on pinball loss <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib141" title="" class="ltx_ref">52</a>]</cite>, averaged across 10
quantile levels <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in\{0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.9\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\in\{0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.9\}</annotation></semantics></math>. We compare against four baselines spanning the typical strategies for quantile regression: a linear quantile regressor, which fits a separate pinball-loss model per quantile level; XGBoost in quantile mode, which uses a single multi-output booster but adds one tree per quantile per boosting round, scaling training cost roughly linearly in the number of levels; quantile random forests <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib153" title="" class="ltx_ref">53</a>]</cite>, which train a single MSE-objective forest and read off all quantiles from leaf-level empirical CDFs at no extra training cost; and TabICL-v2, a tabular foundation model with a quantile head.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN-3 achieves a normalized pinball loss score very close to <math id="S3.SS2.SSS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1.00" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1.00</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1.00</annotation></semantics></math>, ranking first overall
and outperforming all baselines, demonstrating that the bar-distribution head produces
well-calibrated predictive distributions superior to dedicated quantile regression
baselines at no additional training cost per quantile level. The normalized Pinball loss is shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F19" title="Figure 19 ‣ 3.2.3 Many Features ‣ 3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>, while the corresponding Critical Difference plot can be found in the Appendix in Figure <a href="#A6.F35" title="Figure 35 ‣ F.4 Quantile Regression: Critical Difference Diagram ‣ Appendix F Additional Details on Internal Benchmarks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">35</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Time-Series Forecasting</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to the classification and regression checkpoints, we
release a new TabPFN-3 checkpoint for TabPFN-TS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> fine-tuned on <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">synthetic</span> time-series data for
probabilistic time-series forecasting. This checkpoint can be used in our <a href="https://github.com/PriorLabs/tabpfn-time-series" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href ltx_font_typewriter">tabpfn-time-series</a> library. We evaluate it on fev-bench <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib137" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>, a benchmark containing 100 diverse time-series forecasting tasks.
Following this benchmark, we report win rates and skill scores relative to the Seasonal Naive baseline in Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Time-Series Forecasting ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> (full version in Appendix Table <a href="#A8.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Full leaderboards (SQL and MASE) ‣ Appendix H Detailed Time-Series Forecasting Results on fev-bench" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.T1" class="ltx_table">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="S1.T1.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 1</span>: </span><span id="S1.T1.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Forecasting performance on fev-bench (100 tasks),
sorted by skill score.
<span id="S1.T1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TabPFN-TS-3 ranks 2nd among foundation models on both SQL and MASE skill score while being trained only on synthetic data.</span>
The full 18-baseline leaderboard can be found in Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Detailed Time-Series Forecasting Results on fev-bench" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>.</span></figcaption><div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
