</div></div></div>
</figure><span id="footnotex1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnotetext"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">2</sup><span class="ltx_note_type">footnotetext: </span>The fev-bench
authors report 28.8 MASE skill for the original TabPFN-TS
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib137" title="" class="ltx_ref">54</a>]</cite>; our re-run in Table <a href="#A8.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Full leaderboards (SQL and MASE) ‣ Appendix H Detailed Time-Series Forecasting Results on fev-bench" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>
yields 27.6 — we report our own re-run for like-for-like comparison
across the cohort.</span></span></span>
<figure id="S3.F20" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/rohlik_orders_1D_s0.svg" id="S3.F20.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/334;" width="476" height="334"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F20.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 20</span>: </span><span id="S3.F20.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Qualitative forecast comparison on a fev-bench task (<span id="S3.F20.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rohlik_order_1D</span>).<span id="S3.F20.5.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> Each model column shows the forecast horizon (zoomed to time 880-935) against the held-out ground truth, with the shaded band indicating the 10th-90th quantile. The leftmost panel shows the full training history. MASE and CRPS scores are reported per model. Additional examples, including covariate panels, are in <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Detailed Time-Series Forecasting Results on fev-bench" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Appendix</span> <span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our checkpoint is evaluated with up to 32k historical time steps of
context, well beyond the budgets typically used by patch- or
window-based time-series foundation models.
Compared to the original TabPFN-TS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite> as evaluated
by the fev-bench authors (39.6 SQL skill, 28.8 MASE skill;
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib137" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shchur et al. 54</a></cite>), our fine-tuned variant improves to
<span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">43.1 SQL skill</span> and <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">30.6 MASE skill</span>. On the full
100-task cohort it ranks 2nd on mean SQL skill scores (ahead of TiRex and TimesFM-2.5)
and 2nd on MASE (ahead of TimesFM-2.5, which has <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10\%</annotation></semantics></math> flagged
train/test leakage, and TiRex), in both cases behind only Chronos-2.
Looking at the win-rate results, TabPFN-TS-3’s ranking drops to the 4th place, although we found these rates to be very sensitive to tiny differences on a few datasets.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The strong performance of TabPFN-TS-3 is particularly noteworthy seeing that it is trained purely on synthetic data, while most other time-series models, including Chronos-2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib274" title="" class="ltx_ref">55</a>]</cite>, TiRex <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib273" title="" class="ltx_ref">56</a>]</cite> and TimesFM-2.5 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib275" title="" class="ltx_ref">57</a>]</cite> are trained on real-world data. This property of our model prevents many issues from real-data pretraining: historical series are leaky and frequently recirculated across forecasting libraries (fev-bench flags 10% leakage in TimesFM-2.5 and 28% in Moirai-2.0; see Table <a href="#S1.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Time-Series Forecasting ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>), forecasting the future from historical pretraining is fundamentally out-of-distribution, and the supply of public real-world time-series data is finite, so any model relying on it inherits both its biases and its ceiling. Our synthetic prior by design has zero contamination from any specific real time series.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">We also show qualitative examples in Figure <a href="#S3.F20" title="Figure 20 ‣ 3.3 Time-Series Forecasting ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a> to give a better intuition of our model forecasts. Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Detailed Time-Series Forecasting Results on fev-bench" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a> complements this section with the full
leaderboards (Table <a href="#A8.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Full leaderboards (SQL and MASE) ‣ Appendix H Detailed Time-Series Forecasting Results on fev-bench" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a>), pairwise comparisons (Figure <a href="#A8.F45" title="Figure 45 ‣ Pairwise skill-score heatmaps ‣ Appendix H Detailed Time-Series Forecasting Results on fev-bench" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">45</span></a>), additional qualitative forecasts and per-task SQL results.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Relational Data</h3>

<figure id="S3.F21" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F21.fig1" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/relbench_v1_classification_xticks.svg" id="S3.F21.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/373;" width="476" height="373"></object>
</figure></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2">
<figure id="S3.F21.fig2" class="ltx_figure ltx_figure_panel ltx_align_center"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/relbench_v1_regression.svg" id="S3.F21.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/373;" width="476" height="373"></object>
</figure></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F21.6" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 21</span>: </span><span id="S3.F21.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">TabPFN-3</span><span id="S3.F21.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;"> tops performance on RelBenchV1 among foundation models.<span id="S3.F21.8.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib144" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hudovernik et al. [58]</a></cite>, we report the mean ROC AUC for entity classification and MAE scores for entity regression normalized by LightGBM’s MAE. RelGNN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib150" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite> achieves SOTA performance on both tasks, followed by TabPFN-REL, which sets a new SOTA for foundation models.
Methods marked with <sup id="S3.F21.8.1.1" class="ltx_sup"><span id="S3.F21.8.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">∗</span></sup> in their name (KumoRFMv1, <math id="S3.F21.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{RT}_{\text{zero}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>RT</mtext><mtext>zero</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{RT}_{\text{zero}}</annotation></semantics></math>) indicate methods that are likely following a different evaluation protocol than the one outlined in RelBench, which overestimates model performance.
</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Real-world data is often relational: commercial enterprises, healthcare systems, and financial institutions routinely store their core operational data across multiple interconnected tables in relational databases. Unlocking predictive insights from such data is therefore of substantial practical importance, and requires to reason jointly over heterogeneous tables linked by complex foreign-key relationships. This has motivated the development of dedicated relational foundation models (RFMs) that aim to provide accurate, up-to-date predictions via In-Context Learning (ICL) without the need for costly per-task model training and hyperparameter tuning.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">This has sparked the emergence of dedicated solutions for relational data, e.g., fully supervised solutions particularly tailored for relational data such as GraphSAGE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib149" title="" class="ltx_ref">60</a>]</cite>, RelGT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib151" title="" class="ltx_ref">61</a>]</cite> and RelGNN <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib150" title="" class="ltx_ref">59</a>]</cite>, closed-source relational foundation models like KumoRFMv1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib145" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>]</cite> and KumoRFMv2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib144" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite>, as well as open-source RFMs, Griffin <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib146" title="" class="ltx_ref">63</a>]</cite> and <math id="S3.SS4.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{RT}_{\text{zero}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>RT</mtext><mtext>zero</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{RT}_{\text{zero}}</annotation></semantics></math> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib148" title="" class="ltx_ref">64</a>]</cite>. Recently, RDBLearn <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib147" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>]</cite> has shown that TFMs including TabPFN can be converted into RFMs by automatically flattening the underlying database into a table.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we build on this research and show how <em id="S3.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">TabPFN-REL</em> using TabPFN-3 achieves state of the art performance on the popular RelBenchV1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib152" title="" class="ltx_ref">66</a>]</cite> benchmark for entity classification and regression.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p">For RelBench, we follow the general guidelines by truncating each database at the pre-specified test timestamp before constructing the featurization and context for all test entities. Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib144" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hudovernik et al. [58]</a></cite>, we generally report baseline results as provided by the authors of the methods to ensure well-tuned baselines. For methods that likely follow a different evaluation regime, we rerun the evaluation using RelBench’s data regime, falling back to author-reported numbers where rerunning is not possible due to model deprecation or missing checkpoints (as is the case for KumoRFMv1 and <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{RT}_{\text{zero}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>RT</mtext><mtext>zero</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{RT}_{\text{zero}}</annotation></semantics></math>); we note that these may not be directly comparable due to potentially different data setups. For KumoRFMv2 we adapt the original scripts provided by the authors and use four estimators and a context size of <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="10000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>10000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">10000</annotation></semantics></math> (the respective maxima for each), which we found to slightly outperform the script defaults of one estimator and a context size of <math id="S3.SS4.p4.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="5000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>5000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">5000</annotation></semantics></math> samples. We compare three different versions of RDBLearn: Vanilla RDBLearn that tunes over a range of different TFMs including TabPFN-2.5, as well as versions which forgo the tuning and use either TabPFN-2.5 or <span id="S3.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> as a fixed TFM.<span id="footnote3" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">3</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">3</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            The reported results were produced with early checkpoints that did not undergo the full training pipeline and separate binary from multiclass classification. They can be identified on HuggingFace by the <span id="footnote3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">20260417_&lt;TASK_TYPE&gt;</span> suffix.</span></span></span></p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">TabPFN-REL sets a new state-of-the-art among RFMs.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the aggregate performance of the different RFMs and fully-supervised baselines in <a href="#S3.F21" title="Figure 21 ‣ 3.4 Relational Data ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Figure 21</span></a> both for entity classification and entity regression on RelBenchV1, as well as per-dataset results in <a href="#A5.SS5" title="E.5 Per-dataset results on RelBenchV1 ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">subsection E.5</span></a>. <span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">TabPFN-REL achieves state-of-the-art performance among RFMs on both tasks</span>, with KumoRFMv1/v2 coming second on regression/classification. We attribute KumoRFMv1’s strong classification results in part to a potentially different evaluation regime used by the authors, which likely overestimates performance, especially on the <span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">rel-f1</span> task suite. We also observe that RDBLearn with the fixed TabPFN-3 backend consistently outperforms the original RDBLearn, which itself tunes over various TFMs including TabPFN-2.5. RDBLearn using <span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> hence Pareto-dominates vanilla RDBLearn in terms of runtime and performance, and to the best of our knowledge sets a <span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">new state-of-the-art among open-source RFMs</span>. <span id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">At the time of writing, TabPFN-3 therefore powers both the best overall relational foundation model (TabPFN-REL) and the best open-source alternative (RDBLearn + v3).</span></p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Comparison to fully-supervised baselines.</h5>

<div id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS4.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The fully-supervised RelGNN outperforms TabPFN-REL, with the gap being larger on classification than regression. On regression, the gap between RelGNN and TabPFN-REL is slim, with TabPFN-REL achieving lower mean rank than RelGNN. RelGT and GraphSAGE fall behind TabPFN-REL both in terms of normalized score and rank. We note that training supervised methods is several orders of magnitude more expensive than the in-context learning performed in TabPFN-REL <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib147" title="" class="ltx_ref">65</a>, <a href="#bib.bib145" title="" class="ltx_ref">62</a>, <a href="#bib.bib144" title="" class="ltx_ref">58</a>]</cite>. This is both because training a single supervised model takes significantly longer than the forward pass of TabPFN-REL, and because supervised methods require extensive per-dataset hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance. For example, we identified at least seven axes of variability in RelGNN’s per-dataset configs, yielding thousands of possible hyperparameter combinations to search over.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.5 </span>Causal Inference</h3>

<div id="S3.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We follow up on our previous results <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>, which showed strong performance of TabPFN-2.5 as a meta (T/X/S) learner <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite> on the RealCause benchmark, by providing an evaluation on the <span id="S3.SS5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scikit-uplift</span> benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>]</cite>. In terms of QINI-score, a real-world evaluation strategy for experimental data, we observe that all TabPFN-3 meta-learners improve over TabPFN-2.5, with the top two spots occupied by T and S-Learners (Figure <a href="#A5.F27" title="Figure 27 ‣ Causal Inference. ‣ E.1 Details on Causal Inference Results ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">27</span></a>). In contrast, we observe slightly worse performance compared to TabPFN-2.5 on RealCause <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>.
We provide a more in-depth analysis of the results and description of the QINI evaluation protocol in Appendix <a href="#A5.SS1" title="E.1 Details on Causal Inference Results ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E.1</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.6 </span>Embeddings</h3>

<div id="S3.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Finally, we demonstrate that <span id="S3.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> generates semantically-meaningful embeddings. We follow the approach developed by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib156" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ye et al. [27]</a></cite> for TabPFN v2: we partition the dataset into cross-validation folds, and take the embeddings from the test-portion of the dataset in each fold. The embeddings we capture are the output of the ICL layers at the end of Stage 3 of our model (see Section /<a href="#S2.SS1" title="2.1 Architecture ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.1</span></a> for more details). Figure <a href="#S3.F22" title="Figure 22 ‣ 3.6 Embeddings ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a> shows that this approach continues to work well for TabPFN-3, with the generated embeddings capturing the dataset structure.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F22" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2605.13986v2/embeddings_scatter.png" id="S3.F22.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="width:36.052em; height:20.958em;aspect-ratio:599/348;" width="599" height="348" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="S3.F22.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 22</span>: </span><span id="S3.F22.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">
<span id="S3.F22.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">TabPFN-3 extracts semantically-meaningful row embeddings.</span>
The upper plots show 2D PCA applied directly to three classification datasets, where each point is a row, while the lower plots show PCA applied to embeddings of the rows.
Color indicates the class.
We observe that the embeddings are clustered by class.
</span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Adoption</h2>

<div id="S4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN-3 is shipped into an already sprawling ecosystem. Since the v2 release, TabPFN has been picked up across academic ML research, applied science, and enterprise deployment. A substantial portion of the extension work referenced throughout this report (time-series, causal inference, relational data, interpretability) was driven by that community rather than initiated internally. This section describes the shape of that adoption – where the model is in production, where it is being evaluated, which platforms make it accessible, and which research areas have published applications – to give the v3 release its actual operational context.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Community and Open-Source Ecosystem</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The open-source <span id="S4.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tabpfn</span> package has surpassed 3.2 million PyPI downloads, and the original TabPFN Nature paper <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> has been cited in over 1,000 papers in the sixteen months since publication.<span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">4</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">4</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            Google Scholar entry and pepy.tech <span id="footnote4.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tabpfn</span> download statistics, both accessed May 8, 2026.</span></span></span> A Discord community of over 2,000 users and hundreds of resolved GitHub issues have driven cross-platform stability work, edge-case fixes, and the maturation of the model from research artifact to production-grade library.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">A separate <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">tabpfn-extensions</span> repository<span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">5</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">5</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/PriorLabs/tabpfn-extensions" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/PriorLabs/tabpfn-extensions</a></span></span></span> hosts community-driven extensions that compose with the core model: SHAP and SHAP-IQ interpretability, synthetic data generation and missing-value imputation, TabPFN-based feature selection, regression-via-classification, survival analysis and conditional randomization tests. TabPFN-3’s reduced KV cache and inference improvements (Section <a href="#S2" title="2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) directly accelerate every extension that depends on repeated forward passes – most notably interpretability and conditional independence testing.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN also serves as a foundational layer for methods published as independent research, spanning time-series forecasting <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">19</a>]</cite>, node classification on graphs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">24</a>, <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">25</a>]</cite>, evolving data streams <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">70</a>]</cite>, causal inference <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">20</a>, <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">21</a>, <a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">22</a>]</cite>, reinforcement learning <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">28</a>]</cite>, high-dimensional Bayesian optimization <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">23</a>]</cite>, and multimodal encoding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">71</a>]</cite>. As shown in Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, many of these extensions move further forward when run with TabPFN-3 as the backend rather than v2.5 or v2.6.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Enterprise Engagements</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN has been deployed and evaluated across a wide range of enterprise settings. Examples include: <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Hitachi Rail</span> deploys TabPFN for predictive maintenance on the Spanish rail network; in initial deployment, TabPFN reduced root-mean-square error by approximately 40% compared to their existing baseline <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">72</a>]</cite>. <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Creditplus Bank</span>, part of the Crédit Agricole group, will use distilled TabPFN models (Section <a href="#S2.SS4.SSS3" title="2.4.3 Model Distillation ‣ 2.4 Inference Optimization ‣ 2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2.4.3</span></a>) for assisting CPU-based credit decisioning in motor finance under appropriate credit-risk regulatory constraints <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">73</a>]</cite>. <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Oxford Cancer Analytics</span> applies TabPFN to proteomic liquid-biopsy data for early lung-disease detection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">74</a>]</cite>. A longer list of enterprise and commercial engagements is available on the Prior Labs website.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Platform Availability</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TabPFN is available through the open-source PyPI distribution for evaluation and non-commercial use, and through a managed API for commercial workloads. The model is currently listed on the <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">AWS SageMaker Marketplace<span id="footnote6" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">6</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">6</span></span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-chfhncrdzlb3s" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_upright">https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-chfhncrdzlb3s</a></span></span></span></span> and the <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Azure AI Foundry Model Catalog<span id="footnote7" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">7</sup>
                <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note"><span id="footnote7.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_upright">7</span></span>
                
                
                
                
                
                
                
              <a href="https://ai.azure.com/catalog/models/TabPFN-2.5" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter ltx_font_upright">https://ai.azure.com/catalog/models/TabPFN-2.5</a></span></span></span></span>, with full support for batch and real-time inference on classification and regression tasks; the TabPFN-3 release on both marketplaces follows this report. A reference integration for <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Databricks</span> is available through the Databricks Industry Solutions repository<span id="footnote8" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">8</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">8</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            <a href="https://github.com/databricks-industry-solutions/tabpfn-databricks" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/databricks-industry-solutions/tabpfn-databricks</a></span></span></span>. See Section <a href="#S5" title="5 License and Availability" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> for license terms, commercial-use scope, and the contact path for production deployment.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Research Adoption Across Domains</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In addition to commercial engagement, we have collected more than 200 published research applications of TabPFN across a broad range of areas; the full list is in Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I TabPFN Use Case Overview" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Adoption is strongest in <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">healthcare and life sciences</span> (98 applications), reflecting TabPFN’s relative advantage in data-scarce settings: diagnosis, prognosis, treatment-response prediction, biomarker modeling, survival analysis, drug discovery, pharmacokinetics, radiomics, omics, and multimodal clinical data. <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Manufacturing and industrial</span> applications (41 papers) span concrete and asphalt strength prediction, geotechnical modeling, tunnel construction, steel and semiconductor properties, IIoT intrusion detection, rotating-machinery fault classification, battery and circuit modeling, and materials discovery. <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Energy and utilities</span> (24 papers) cluster around environmental monitoring, renewable-energy and geophysical prediction, water and climate systems, and industrial process optimization. <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Financial services</span> (7 papers) include transaction analytics, churn prediction, return forecasting, actuarial modeling, and credit-risk prediction; the relatively small published count almost certainly underrepresents commercial traction in a domain that publishes little. The remaining 32 applications span uncertainty estimation, hypothesis testing, Shapley value estimation, graph node classification, cybersecurity, geoscience, agriculture, soil and lunar-regolith analysis, fuel-blend prediction, crop-yield forecasting, forensic ancestry prediction, and synthetic tabular data generation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The distribution of these applications – weighted toward domains characterized by limited, expensive, or heterogeneous data – is consistent with the regime TabPFN was designed for, and is the empirical basis for the v3 capability choices described in Section <a href="#S2" title="2 TabPFN-3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>License and Availability</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We release TabPFN-3 under the <span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TABPFN-3.0 License v1.0</span>, designed to be permissive for academic use, research, and evaluation in commercial settings. The license <em id="S5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">explicitly allows</em> testing, evaluation, and internal benchmarking, so an organization can download the model and run preliminary assessments on its own datasets without a commercial agreement.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The key restriction is that the model, its derivatives, and its outputs cannot be used for commercial or production purposes. This includes, but is not limited to, revenue-generating products, competitive benchmarking for procurement decisions, client deliverables, and using model outputs as inputs to internal commercial decision-making.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For production use, we offer a <em id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">Commercial Enterprise License</em>, available for our managed API, Virtual Private Cloud deployments (at the time of publication: AWS SageMaker &amp; Azure AI Foundry), and on-prem or other custom deployment modes across other software platforms such as Databricks and SAP. The Commercial Enterprise License provides access to our proprietary high-speed inference engine, dedicated support, integration tooling, additional internal models, and the <span id="S5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) variant, which is not available as part of the open-source release. The managed API runs on our optimized GPU infrastructure and is the recommended option for users without dedicated local GPUs; it is accessible via a Python SDK<span id="footnote9" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">9</sup>
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">9</span>
            
            
            
            
            
            
            
          The Python client SDK is available on PyPI: <a href="https://github.com/PriorLabs/tabpfn-client" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/PriorLabs/tabpfn-client</a>.</span></span></span> (<span id="S5.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">pip install tabpfn-client</span>) or a standard REST API.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p4" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The full <span id="S5.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">TABPFN-3.0 License v1.0</span> text is available at <a href="https://huggingface.co/Prior-Labs/tabpfn_3/blob/main/LICENSE" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/Prior-Labs/tabpfn_3/blob/main/LICENSE</a>. For commercial licensing inquiries, please contact <a href="mailto:sales@priorlabs.ai" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_href">sales@priorlabs.ai</a>.</p>
</div>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Prior visualizations</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We provide a number of illustrative visualizations for the improvements to our prior. Figure <a href="#A4.F23" title="Figure 23 ‣ Appendix D Prior visualizations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">23</span></a> shows directed acyclic graphs sampled by our new graph-sampling algorithms; Figure <a href="#A4.F24" title="Figure 24 ‣ Appendix D Prior visualizations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">24</span></a> visualizes the functional relationships generated by the new combiner mechanisms;
Figure <a href="#A4.F25.fig1" title="Figure 25 ‣ Appendix D Prior visualizations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">25</span></a> gives an example classification dataset generated from the prior; and Figure <a href="#A4.F26" title="Figure 26 ‣ Appendix D Prior visualizations" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">26</span></a> demonstrates TabPFN-3’s extrapolation capabilities, comparing to CatBoost.</p>
</div>

<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Experimental results details</h2>

<section id="A5.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.1 </span>Details on Causal Inference Results</h3>

<section id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Causal Inference.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Many practical problems are rooted in causal logic, requiring an understanding of how interventions, rather than mere associations, shape outcomes. Estimating Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATEs) serves as a primary tool for addressing these "what-if" scenarios, quantifying the expected change in an individual’s response when a treatment is applied compared to when it is withheld. Previous results <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite> have shown that TabPFN-2.5, especially when used as a T-Learner <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">67</a>]</cite>, achieves SOTA performance on the RealCause benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>. While TabPFN-3 does not quite achieve the highest performance on RealCause (still surpassed by TabPFN-2.5), we see substantial improvements on larger datasets with up to 50k samples in the <span id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scikit-uplift</span> library <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>]</cite>. We describe the details of this evaluation below.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F27" class="ltx_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_figure">
<div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2605.13986v2/figures/causal/uplift.png" id="A5.F27.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:234/178;" width="234" height="178" alt="Refer to caption"></div><div class="ltx_flex_cell ltx_flex_size_2"><img src="2605.13986v2/figures/causal/RealCause.png" id="A5.F27.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_figure_panel ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:234/178;" width="234" height="178" alt="Refer to caption"></div></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F27.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 27</span>: </span><span id="A5.F27.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">TabPFN-3 as a T/X/S-Learner.<span id="A5.F27.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> TabPFN-3 when used as a T/S-Learner achieves strong performance in terms of QINI-score (<math id="A5.F27.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\uparrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↑</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\uparrow</annotation></semantics></math>) in Uplift Modeling on the <span id="A5.F27.6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scikit-uplift</span> benchmark. We report worsened performance in terms of PEHE (<math id="A5.F27.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\downarrow" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo stretchy="false">↓</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\downarrow</annotation></semantics></math>) on the RealCause benchmark compared to the previous version.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Real-World QINI Evaluation.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">One of the major drawbacks in evaluating causal inference methods is referred to by <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Holland [75]</a></cite> as the Fundamental Problem of Causal Inference, which states that individual treatment effects can never actually be observed in the real-world. In simple terms, one cannot experimentally test both potential outcomes without interference. Under the assumption of experimental (RCT) data, Uplift Modeling <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">68</a>]</cite> allows to evaluate the benefit of using a causal estimator in terms of ranking individuals by treatment effect. Crucially, this evaluation strategy does not require access to ground truth (synthetic) treatment effects, and serves as arguably the most real-world evaluation of CATE estimators, for example, when A/B testing data is available. Using only observed treatment and outcomes, one can compute the Area-Under the QINI Curve (AUC-QINI) to evaluate CATE estimators by their ability to identify individuals for which the treatment has a strong impact.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Strong Performance in Uplift Modeling.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report the mean normalized AUC-QINI score for the T/X/S meta-learners using TabPFN-2.5 and 3 (Figure <a href="#A5.F27" title="Figure 27 ‣ Causal Inference. ‣ E.1 Details on Causal Inference Results ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">27</span></a>). TabPFN-3 used as an S and T-Learner achieves stronger performance than other baselines. We observe somewhat worsened performance on the RealCause benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">69</a>]</cite>, which is characterized by smaller sample sizes.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.2 </span>Detailed TabArena Results</h3>

<section id="A5.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">E.2.1 </span>Evaluation Metrics</h4>

<div id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We re-use the official TabArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite> evaluation metrics and code for generating TabArena plots and tables.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Elo</span>: Following TabArena, we evaluate models using the Elo rating system <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib271" title="" class="ltx_ref">76</a>]</cite>. Elo is a pairwise
comparison-based rating system where each model’s rating predicts its expected win probability against others, with a 400-point Elo gap corresponding to a 10 to 1 (91%) expected win rate. We calibrate 1000 Elo to the performance of the default TabArena random forest configuration across all figures, and perform 200 rounds of bootstrapping to obtain 95% confidence intervals, similar to what is done in ChatBot Arena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib272" title="" class="ltx_ref">77</a>]</cite>. In our TabArena results, Elo scores are computed using ROC AUC for binary classification, log-loss for multiclass classification, and RMSE for regression.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Improvability</span>: The improvability metric introduced in TabArena measures how many percent lower the error of the best method is than the current method on a dataset. This is then averaged over datasets. Formally, for a single dataset,</p>
<table id="A5.Ex2" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A5.Ex2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\operatorname{Improvability}:=\frac{\operatorname{err}_{i}-\operatorname{best\_err}_{i}}{\operatorname{err}_{i}}\cdot 100\%~." display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>Improvability</mi><mo>:=</mo><mrow><mfrac><mrow><msub><mi>err</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo lspace="0em">−</mo><msub><mrow><mi>best</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>err</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><msub><mi>err</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mfrac><mo lspace="0.222em" rspace="0.222em">⋅</mo><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo rspace="0.052em">%</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><mo>.</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\operatorname{Improvability}:=\frac{\operatorname{err}_{i}-\operatorname{best\_err}_{i}}{\operatorname{err}_{i}}\cdot 100\%~.</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Improvability is always between <math id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="0\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0\%</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="A5.SS2.SSS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100\%" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100\%</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">E.2.2 </span>Experiment Details</h4>

<div id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For all TabArena results, we run experiments using the official TabArena code and evaluation pipeline. We will contribute a reproducible official TabArena submission for <span id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> shortly after it becomes publicly available. While not strictly necessary to make predictions on test data, we follow TabArena’s fit time procedure of fitting an 8-fold bagged ensemble to generate a cross-validation score followed by refitting the model on the full training data at test time, as is done for the other tabular foundation models on TabArena.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">All results for non-<span id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> models in our TabArena experiments were from the official TabArena reported results. All cached results from tabular foundation models (TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-2.6, TabICLv2 and TabDPT) were run on a single H200 GPU, while all results for <span id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> and <span id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) were run on a single RTX 6000 GPU, a weaker GPU compared to an H200.</p>
</div>
<div id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">For both <span id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3</span> and <span id="A5.SS2.SSS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking), we ran all splits of TabArena, which includes a total of 816 tasks across 51 datasets. In all cases we report results for all splits of each dataset.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">E.2.3 </span>TabArena Pareto Frontier Explanation</h4>

<div id="A5.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S0.F3" title="Figure 3" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S3.F12" title="Figure 12 ‣ 3.1.1 TabArena ‣ 3.1 Public Tabular Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> show TabArena Pareto frontiers of models across Improvability and the median combined train + inference time per 1000 samples. The connected points for a given model type indicate tuning + ensembling performance with points from left to right marking ensembles of increasing numbers of random configurations (1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100, 150, 201). The trajectories are sampled 20 times from all
trials and averaged. The left-most points use the default configuration, and the right-most highlighted points use all configurations.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A5.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.3 </span>Details on TALENT benchmark results</h3>

<section id="A5.SS3.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">E.3.1 </span>Benchmark description</h4>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">TALENT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib140" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> base contains 300 datasets (120 binary, 80 multiclass, 100 regression).
Each dataset is split into 64% training, 16% validation, and 20% test sets.</p>
</div>
<section id="A5.SS3.SSS1.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Baselines.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS1.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We rely on precomputed baselines provided by the authors of
the TALENT benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib140" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> (for the TALENT extensions which we
use for the large-rows slice and the many-class slice) or the TabICLv2 paper
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite> (for the main TALENT slice).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3.SSS1.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metrics.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS1.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS1.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following the TALENT paper and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, we use accuracy for classification and rmse for regression.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3.SSS1.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Datasets.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS1.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS1.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Following <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib139" title="" class="ltx_ref">30</a>]</cite>, we exclude the 26 development datasets used for
TabPFN-2 / TabICLv2 development from the main TALENT benchmark.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">E.3.2 </span>Per-task-type breakdown</h4>

<figure id="A5.F28" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/by_task_average_rank_paper.svg" id="A5.F28.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/346;" width="476" height="346"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F28.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 28</span>: </span><span id="A5.F28.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Average rank on the TALENT benchmark broken down by task type
(regression, binary classification, multiclass classification), using the

</section>
<section id="A5.SS3.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">E.3.3 </span>Many-class TALENT subset</h4>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report results on the subset of TALENT <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib140" title="" class="ltx_ref">38</a>]</cite> datasets with more than <math id="A5.SS3.SSS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="50" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>50</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">50</annotation></semantics></math> classes, which yields 4 datasets with 100 classes, including 3 from the same family. While limited in number, these complement the results on synthetic data from Section <a href="#S3.SS2.SSS2" title="3.2.2 Many-Class Classification ‣ 3.2 Internal Benchmarks ‣ 3 Experimental Results" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3.2.2</span></a>. Results are shown in Figure <a href="#A5.F29" title="Figure 29 ‣ E.3.3 Many-class TALENT subset ‣ E.3 Details on TALENT benchmark results ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">29</span></a>.</p>

<section id="A5.SS3.SSS5" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">E.3.5 </span>Details</h4>

<section id="A5.SS3.SSS5.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Per-dataset ranking.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS5.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS5.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">For each (dataset, split) we rank all
methods by their score (best <math id="A5.SS3.SSS5.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mphantom></mphantom><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=1</annotation></semantics></math>; ties get average ranks). The reported
<em id="A5.SS3.SSS5.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_emph ltx_font_italic">mean rank</em> of a method is the average of these for ranks across all
(dataset, split) pairs in the slice.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS3.SSS5.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Bootstrap confidence intervals.</h5>

<div id="A5.SS3.SSS5.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS3.SSS5.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">95% confidence intervals are
non-parametric bootstrap over datasets: for each of <math id="A5.SS3.SSS5.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="B=2{,}000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2,000</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">B=2{,}000</annotation></semantics></math>
replicates we resample the (dataset, split) pairs with replacement and
recompute each method’s mean rank, then take the empirical <math id="A5.SS3.SSS5.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="2.5/97.5" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>2.5</mn><mo>/</mo><mn>97.5</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">2.5/97.5</annotation></semantics></math>
percentiles across replicates.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A5.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">E.4 </span>Details on TabSTAR Text-Tabular Benchmark results</h3>

<div id="A5.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The TabSTAR benchmark is a union of previous text-tabular benchmarks: the Multimodal AutoML Benchmark <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">49</a>]</cite>,
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Grinsztajn et al. [50]</a></cite>, and CARTE <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">51</a>]</cite>. After deduplication and exclusion of unavailable datasets, the final benchmark contains 50 datasets: 15 classification and 35 regression tasks.<span id="footnote10" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">10</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">10</span>
              
              
              
              
              
              
              
            The TabSTAR paper reports 14 classification tasks, having mistakenly treated <span id="footnote10.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Spotify Genres</span> as a regression dataset.</span></span></span> Each model is run 5 times, with per-task metrics AUROC (binary classification), log-loss (multiclass), and RMSE (regression); results are normalized with MinMax scaling to the <math id="A5.SS4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> range. As in the original paper
<cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">39</a>]</cite>, we limit each run to up to 100,000 examples. Figure <a href="#A5.F31" title="Figure 31 ‣ E.4 Details on TabSTAR Text-Tabular Benchmark results ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">31</span></a> shows the results for
classification, for which the TabSTAR model was reportedly the state of the art; we see that the TabPFN API family significantly outperforms
it. Figure <a href="#A5.F32" title="Figure 32 ‣ E.4 Details on TabSTAR Text-Tabular Benchmark results ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">32</span></a> shows the equivalent regression performance.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.F31" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/tabstar_classification.svg" id="A5.F31.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/200;" width="381" height="200"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F31.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 31</span>: </span><span id="A5.F31.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Performance on the classification tasks of the TabSTAR text-tabular collection.<span id="A5.F31.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <span id="A5.F31.6.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) and TabPFN-3-Plus significantly
outperform the text-aware TabSTAR, which was otherwise the state-of-the-art reference for this task type.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
<figure id="A5.F32" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/tabstar_regression.svg" id="A5.F32.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:381/200;" width="381" height="200"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A5.F32.5" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 32</span>: </span><span id="A5.F32.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Performance on the regression tasks of the TabSTAR text-tabular collection.<span id="A5.F32.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> <span id="A5.F32.6.1.1" class="ltx_text">TabPFN-3-Plus</span> (Thinking) and TabPFN-3-Plus significantly
outperform all baselines.</span></span></figcaption>
</figure>
</section>

<p id="A5.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We report per-dataset results for entity regression and entity classification as well as aggregate metrics in <a href="#A5.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ E.5 Per-dataset results on RelBenchV1 ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 14</span></a> and <a href="#A5.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ E.5 Per-dataset results on RelBenchV1 ‣ Appendix E Experimental results details" class="ltx_ref ltx_refmacro_autoref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">Table 15</span></a>, respectively.</p>

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix F </span>Additional Details on Internal Benchmarks</h2>

<section id="A6.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.1 </span>Methodology</h3>

<section id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Metric Normalization.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To aggregate heterogeneous metrics across datasets, we apply a per-fold min–max normalization.
For each (dataset, fold) pair and metric <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="m" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>m</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">m</annotation></semantics></math>, we rescale a model’s raw score <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="s_{m}^{(b)}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">s_{m}^{(b)}</annotation></semantics></math> as</p>
<table id="A6.E1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="A6.E1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{s}_{m}^{(b)}=\frac{s_{m}^{(b)}-\min_{b^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}}\,s_{m}^{(b^{\prime})}}{\max_{b^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}}\,s_{m}^{(b^{\prime})}-\min_{b^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}}\,s_{m}^{(b^{\prime})}}," display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><msubsup><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow><mrow><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.337em">⁡</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><msub><mi>min</mi><mrow><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo>∈</mo><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi></mrow></msub><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><msubsup><mi>s</mi><mi>m</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>b</mi><mo>′</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mrow></mfrac></mrow><mo>,</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{s}_{m}^{(b)}=\frac{s_{m}^{(b)}-\min_{b^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}}\,s_{m}^{(b^{\prime})}}{\max_{b^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}}\,s_{m}^{(b^{\prime})}-\min_{b^{\prime}\in\mathcal{B}}\,s_{m}^{(b^{\prime})}},</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td>
<td rowspan="1" class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_eqno ltx_align_middle ltx_align_right"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_equation ltx_align_right">(1)</span></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{B}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℬ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{B}</annotation></semantics></math> denotes the set of models we evaluate. This allows the model scores to live on a comparable <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="[0,1]" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">]</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">[0,1]</annotation></semantics></math> scale for each (dataset, fold) combination. We treat the tuned and default versions of a model as two different models.
For lower-is-better metrics (e.g. RMSE, cross-entropy loss), we apply the additional transformation <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\tilde{s}_{m}\mapsto 1-\tilde{s}_{m}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">↦</mo><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>−</mo><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>~</mo></mover><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\tilde{s}_{m}\mapsto 1-\tilde{s}_{m}</annotation></semantics></math>, so that all metrics are higher-is-better on a common scale and can be meaningfully averaged or ranked across datasets and metric types.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h5 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Statistical significance.</h5>

<div id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To assess whether performance differences between models are statistically significant, we report critical difference (CD) diagrams using <span id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scikit-posthocs</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib154" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>]</cite>.
The critical difference diagram from <span id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">scikit-posthocs</span> summarizes the statistical comparison of methods across multiple datasets. Average ranks are computed per method across all datasets, with lower ranks indicating better performance.
Methods connected by a horizontal bar are not significantly different from each other.
To assess statistical significance, we use a Friedman test followed by a Conover post hoc analysis at the significance level <math id="A6.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.05</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A6.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.2 </span>Large Data Benchmark Details</h3>

<div id="A6.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Classification datasets span domains including healthcare (patient
survival, disease diagnosis), customer analytics (satisfaction, credit risk), insurance
(claim prediction), microfinance (loan outcomes), and high-energy physics
(signal/background classification). Regression datasets cover retail sales forecasting,
climate and weather modeling, food delivery logistics, and e-commerce price prediction. All 4 regression datasets use temporal train/test splits reflecting real-world
deployment conditions where the test period strictly follows the training period. For classification, all datasets are IID. These datasets are selected to have between 100K and 1M training rows, and fewer than 200 features, which is the regime TabPFN-3 was designed for.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Figures <a href="#A6.F33" title="Figure 33 ‣ F.2 Large Data Benchmark Details ‣ Appendix F Additional Details on Internal Benchmarks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">33</span></a> and <a href="#A6.F34" title="Figure 34 ‣ F.2 Large Data Benchmark Details ‣ Appendix F Additional Details on Internal Benchmarks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">34</span></a> show critical difference
diagrams for ROC-AUC and RMSE respectively, based on average ranks across all datasets in
each benchmark.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.F33" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/big_data_cls_v2_wo_AG__roc_auc__cd_scikit_posthocs.svg" id="A6.F33.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/169;" width="476" height="169"></object>

</section>
<section id="A6.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.3 </span>Synthetic Many-Class Benchmark Construction</h3>

<div id="A6.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Continuous regression targets are partitioned into <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=100" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=100</annotation></semantics></math> bins using quantile-based
bin edges whose spacings are drawn from a <math id="A6.SS3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathrm{Dirichlet}(\alpha{=}5.0)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>Dirichlet</mi><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5.0</mn></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathrm{Dirichlet}(\alpha{=}5.0)</annotation></semantics></math>
distribution, producing realistic class imbalance. Bins with fewer than 10 samples are merged
with their nearest neighbour to guarantee sufficient representation for inner cross-validations.
Class labels are then randomly permuted to remove the implicit ordinal structure inherited from the regression target.</p>
</div>
<div id="A6.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A6.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">tasets from TabArena whose targets have heavy point masses or too few distinct values to fill 100 quantile bins meaningfully — wine_quality (7 unique values), Food_Delivery_Time (45, discrete times), Fiat-500 (222, discrete prices), and QSAR-TID-11 (concentrated point masses). Dataset statistics are reported in Table <a href="#A6.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ F.3 Synthetic Many-Class Benchmark Construction ‣ Appendix F Additional Details on Internal Benchmarks" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a>. The resulting benchmark retains a large number of classes for most datasets (median <math id="A6.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K=95" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>95</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K=95</annotation></semantics></math>), while inducing moderate class imbalance (median IR <math id="A6.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_math_unparsed" alttext="=9.9\times" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>9.9</mn><mo lspace="0.222em">×</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">=9.9\times</annotation></semantics></math>) without collapsing the label distribution onto a few dominant classes (median <math id="A6.SS3.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H/\log K=0.98" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mrow><mo>=</mo><mn>0.98</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H/\log K=0.98</annotation></semantics></math>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="A6.T16" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table"><span id="A6.T16.8" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Table 16</span>: </span><span id="A6.T16.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Synthetic many-class benchmark datasets derived from continuous regression targets.<span id="A6.T16.9.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
<math id="A6.T16.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> is the number of samples before binning. Targets are first partitioned into
100 quantile-based bins with randomized Dirichlet-spaced bin widths, after which
bins with fewer than 10 samples are merged into their nearest neighbour. <math id="A6.T16.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>K</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">K</annotation></semantics></math> is
the resulting number of classes and </span>Merged<span id="A6.T16.9.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> equals <math id="A6.T16.m8" class="ltx_Math" alttext="100-K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>−</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">100-K</annotation></semantics></math>. </span>Min<span id="A6.T16.9.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium">
and </span>Max<span id="A6.T16.9.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> are the smallest and largest class sizes after merging, and
</span>IR<span id="A6.T16.9.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> is their ratio. <math id="A6.T16.m9" class="ltx_Math" alttext="H/\log K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>H</mi><mo>/</mo><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">H/\log K</annotation></semantics></math> is the Shannon entropy of the class
distribution normalized by <math id="A6.T16.m10" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\log K" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>log</mi><mo lspace="0.167em">⁡</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\log K</annotation></semantics></math>, with 1 corresponding to perfectly balanced
classes.
</span></span></figcaption>
<div id="A6.T16.10" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_center ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:345.0pt;height:71.8pt;vertical-align:-34.6pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-148.5pt,30.9pt) scale(0.537417358418667,0.537417358418667) ;">

<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">F.4 </span>Quantile Regression: Critical Difference Diagram</h3>

<figure id="A6.F35" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2605.13986v2/tabarena_regression__pinball_loss__cd_scikit_posthocs.svg" id="A6.F35.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/164;" width="476" height="164"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure"><span id="A6.F35.4" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:90%;">Figure 35</span>: </span><span id="A6.F35.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="font-size:90%;">Critical difference diagram for pinball loss on our quantile regression benchmark.<span id="A6.F35.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_medium"> The quantile regression benchmark is constructed from TabArena regression datasets and evaluated
across 10 quantile levels <math id="A6.F35.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="q\in\{0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.9\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>∈</mo><mrow><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">{</mo><mrow><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">…</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow><mo maxsize="1.110em" minsize="1.110em">}</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">q\in\{0.1,0.2,\ldots,0.9\}</annotation></semantics></math>.
TabPFN-3 ranks first. Its rank difference to Quantile TabICLv2 is not
statistically significant, while it ranks significantly ahead of all
remaining baselines. Bars connect methods whose rank differences are not
statistically significant at <math id="A6.F35.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\alpha=0.05" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>α</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.05</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\alpha=0.05</annotation></semantics></math> under a Conover-Friedman
post-hoc test <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">[<a href="#bib.bib154" title="" class="ltx_ref">78</a>]</cite>.
